chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Safwan, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Umar ibn Hanzala who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about two men from our companions who had a dispute between them regarding a debt or inheritance, and they both sought judgment from the Sultan (ruling authority) or the judges. Is that permissible?

So he said: Whoever seeks judgment from the Taghut and it rules in his favor, then he has only taken ill-gotten gains, even if his right was proven — because he accepted it by the ruling of the Taghut, and God has commanded that it be denied.

I said: How should they both proceed? He said: They should seek out the one among you who has narrated our hadiths, has studied our permissibles and our forbidden, and knows our rulings. Then accept him as an arbitrator, for I have indeed appointed him as a judge over you.

And when he judges by our ruling and it is not accepted from him, then it is God's judgment that has been treated with contempt and against us has been the rejection — and the one who rejects us is the one who rejects God, and he is at the boundary of associating partners with God.

key_terms.الشِّرْك: Shirk — associating partners with God; the hadith places rejection of the Imam-appointed judge at this level of severity
key_terms.حاكم: Hakim — ruler or judge; the Imam delegated this authority to qualified scholars
key_terms.حَكَم: Hakam — an arbitrator or adjudicator; in this context, a Shia jurist appointed by the Imam to resolve disputes
key_terms.سحت: Suht — ill-gotten gains; forbidden wealth acquired through impermissible means
key_terms.طاغوت: Taghut — an illegitimate ruling authority; in the Quran and hadith, refers to any authority other than God or His appointed representatives

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Sadiq say about seeking judgment from unjust authorities?
ai.summary: This is the famous 'maqbula' hadith of Umar ibn Hanzala, one of the foundational texts for the doctrine of wilayat al-faqih (guardianship of the jurist) in Shia jurisprudence. Imam Sadiq (AS) forbids Shia Muslims from seeking judgment from unjust ruling authorities (the 'Taghut'), even when their rights are legally valid, because accepting such a judgment through illegitimate channels nullifies its moral basis. In the second part, the Imam provides an alternative: seek a qualified jurist who has studied the Imams' teachings, and he carries delegated judicial authority — rejecting his rulings based on Imamic law is tantamount to rejecting God Himself.
